standard.title: Draw geographical conclusions
standard.description: draw conclusions based on the analysis of the data and information
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have prior evidence-based conclusion skills from F–6 HASS (AC9HS6S05: develop evidence-based conclusions). This standard requires them to draw conclusions specifically in a geographical inquiry context — using geographical concepts (place, space, environment, interconnections, sustainability, scale, change) as organisers, and connecting conclusions to the impacts of geographical phenomena on people, places and environments.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students draw conclusions based on the analysis of geographical data and information.

nodes.label: Geographical concepts as conclusion organisers
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use at least one geographical concept (place, space, environment, interconnections, sustainability, scale or change) to organise and frame a geographical conclusion.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify which geographical concept is most relevant to organising their conclusion and explain why.
nodes.typical_width: Students draw on analysis results and use at least one of the concepts of place, space, environment, interconnections, sustainability, scale or change to organise a response to a geographical inquiry question — e.g. using distribution analysis to form conclusions about sustainability of farming, or using location analysis to form conclusions about interconnections between people, place, environment and liveability.
wider: Apply two different geographical concepts to the same analysis and compare the conclusions each organiser generates — examine how concept choice shapes what the conclusion highlights
Develop a conclusion about interconnections that traces a chain: geographical distribution → human access → social outcome — making explicit how the concept of interconnections connects these
Practise applying each of the seven geographical concepts to a single dataset and evaluate which produces the most insightful conclusion
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who skip the concept organiser step produce conclusions that are empirical summaries ('the data shows X') rather than geographical conclusions ('this distribution pattern shows that sustainability is compromised because…'). The concept organiser is what makes a conclusion geographical rather than generic.

response_modes.reason: The move from analysis results to a geographically-framed conclusion requires explicit practice with the concept organiser as a tool. Scaffold: analysis finding → which concept applies → how does the concept frame a conclusion → what does the conclusion state?

success_criteria: Names the geographical concept used to organise the conclusion and explains how it frames the analytical finding.
Produces a conclusion that is structured by a geographical concept, not just a summary of data findings.

nodes.label: Explaining impacts on people, places and environments
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the impacts of a geographical phenomenon or challenge on people, places and environments, drawing on analysis results.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain at least one impact on people AND one impact on places or environments from their analysis, connected to the geographical phenomenon studied.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain the impacts of a geographical phenomenon or challenge on people, places and environments — e.g. impacts of water scarcity on individuals, communities and government; or impacts of declining water quality on people and liveability of places — connecting each impact to the analytical evidence.
wider: Trace a cascade of impacts: initial geographical phenomenon → first-order impact → second-order impact → systemic consequence — e.g. drought → reduced farm income → community service decline → population loss
Compare impacts at different scales — individual, community, government — and explain how scale shapes the nature and severity of impact
Examine cases where impacts are distributed unequally across groups — who bears the impact and why — connecting to broader geographical concepts of equity and sustainability

response_modes.reason: Explaining impacts across people, places AND environments — not just one category — requires deliberate widening. Students default to human impacts. Using case studies where environmental impacts are primary (water quality, habitat loss) builds fuller impact analysis.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The three-domain impact framework (people, places, environments) is a transferable geographical analytical structure. Students who can apply it to diverse phenomena — water scarcity, hazards, liveability challenges — have a robust conclusion-writing toolkit.
success_criteria: Explains at least one impact on people and one impact on places or environments, connecting each to the geographical phenomenon studied.
Uses analysis evidence to support each impact claim.

nodes.label: Conclusions as answers to the inquiry question
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can produce a geographical conclusion that directly responds to the inquiry question, synthesising analytical findings into a defensible claim.
nodes.minimum_width: Students produce a conclusion that directly answers the inquiry question and is supported by at least two pieces of analytical evidence.
nodes.typical_width: Students produce a geographical conclusion that: directly responds to the inquiry question, synthesises key analytical findings, uses a geographical concept as organiser, and explains impacts on people, places or environments — presented as a coherent claim rather than a list of findings.
wider: Write a conclusion at two different confidence levels — a strong conclusion when evidence is clear and a hedged conclusion when evidence is partial — practising appropriate epistemic language
Develop a counter-argument to a classmate's conclusion using the same data — examine what the same evidence can support if analysed differently
Compare the conclusion reached through quantitative data analysis with the conclusion suggested by qualitative data (e.g. survey results) for the same inquiry — examine whether they agree

response_modes.reason: Writing a conclusion as a coherent claim rather than a list of findings requires practice. Students need repeated opportunities to draft, receive feedback, and revise conclusions — distinguishing between 'here is what I found' (finding) and 'here is what this means' (conclusion).

success_criteria: Produces a conclusion that directly responds to the inquiry question.
Supports the conclusion with at least two analytical findings, using geographical terminology.
